review.notes: Built on the course: brand equity, CBBE diagnosis, positioning, STP, segmentation bases, five segment tests, segment sizing, insight, positioning statement, frame of reference, POP/POD, three POD tests, reason to believe. Calculations checked. Fictional brand and company.

content.company: Goldfield Foods (fictional); the brand is 'Aurora' cooking oil (fictional), sold in supermarkets and small shops
content.briefing: Aurora is losing share to cheaper imports and to a premium rival. Many shoppers know the name but say it is 'just another oil'. You must diagnose the brand and write a positioning the board will fund.

variants.text: Shoppers pay 10% more for Aurora than for an unbranded oil of the same quality. What does this show?

choices.t: Brand equity: value the name adds
choices.f: A price premium is one sign of brand equity.
Quality is the same; the name explains the gap.
Cost does not explain what shoppers pay.

variants.text: Research: 85% of shoppers know Aurora, but most say it is 'just another oil'. Where is the CBBE gap?

choices.f: Salience is fine; the brand lacks a clear meaning.
85% awareness is already high.
Loyalty cannot be built on a brand with no meaning.

variants.text: What is the correct order of the STP process?

choices.f: Divide the market, choose who to serve, then define your place in their minds.
Positioning needs a chosen target first.
Targeting everyone means positioning for no one.

variants.text: You split buyers by 'health-conscious', 'price-first' and 'big family cooking'. Which segmentation base is this?

choices.f: Needs and lifestyles, not location or income.
Geographic splits by province or city.
Demographic splits by income, age or household size.

variants.text: A segment 'people who love cooking on Sundays' cannot be identified in data or reached by any channel. Which tests fail?

choices.f: If you cannot measure or reach it, you cannot target it.
It may be large; the problem is finding and reaching it.
Attractive is not enough.

variants.text: Big-family segment: 200,000 households, 4 bottles a month each, Kz 1,500 a bottle. Realistic share for Aurora: 10%. What monthly revenue?

choices.f: That is the whole segment, before your share.
A zero is missing: 10% of 1.2 bn is 120 m.

variants.text: Which is a real consumer insight?

choices.t: 'Mothers fry often but fear oil harms the family'
choices.f: Observation, motivation and a tension. It explains behaviour.
A fact, not a human truth with tension.
That is a product claim.

variants.text: Which line is a complete positioning statement?

choices.t: For busy family cooks, Aurora is the oil that fries lighter, as it is cold-filtered
choices.f: Target, frame, point of difference and reason to believe.

choices.t: Aurora is the best quality cooking oil for every family, every day, everywhere
choices.f: No target, no difference, no proof.

choices.t: Aurora cooking oil now comes in a new 2-litre bottle with a stronger handle
choices.f: A product news line, not positioning.

variants.text: Aurora is positioned against 'premium olive oils'. Most buyers compare it with other sunflower oils. What is wrong?

choices.t: The frame of reference is wrong
choices.f: Choose the category buyers actually compare with.
A frame buyers do not use confuses them.
Price is not the issue here.

variants.text: To be considered at all in sunflower oil, Aurora must match: clear bottle, fair price, easy to find. What are these?

choices.f: Must-haves to be in the game, not reasons to choose.
Everyone has them, so they do not differentiate.
RTBs prove a difference.

variants.text: Proposed difference: 'Made with love'. Which test does it fail?

choices.f: Desirable maybe, but not provable or ownable.

choices.t: None; it is warm and friendly
choices.f: Warmth without proof does not differentiate.
The core problem is proof.

variants.text: Proposed difference: 'Fries lighter: absorbs 15% less oil, lab-tested'. Rivals cannot match it soon. Verdict?

choices.f: It passes all three tests.
Make it simple in ads, but the substance is strong.
Rivals cannot match it soon, so it is.

variants.text: Which is a strong reason to believe for 'fries lighter'?

choices.f: True, specific and checkable.
A claim, not proof.
Design does not prove performance.

variants.text: Marketing wants to claim 'healthiest oil in Angola' without data.

choices.t: Refuse: claims must be true and provable
choices.f: Unproven claims risk legal action and trust.
A false claim can destroy brand equity.
Small print does not make it true.

variants.text: Signs that Aurora's brand equity is rising include:

choices.t: Higher price premium and repeat buying
choices.f: Premium, loyalty and lower price sensitivity show equity.
Needing discounts is a sign of weak equity.
Promotion volume can hide weak equity.

variants.text: Known, liked for performance, but buyers feel no attachment. CBBE next step?

choices.f: Move up the pyramid once meaning is clear.

choices.t: Restart with a big awareness campaign
choices.f: Salience is already fine.

choices.t: Cut the price to win attachment
choices.f: Price does not build attachment.

variants.text: The sales team wants Aurora to appeal to 'everyone'. What do you answer?

choices.t: A clear target makes the brand stronger
choices.f: Sacrifice is part of positioning.

choices.t: Agree; more people means more sales
choices.f: Positioning for all ends up meaning nothing.
Not affordable, and it splits focus.

variants.text: Positioning is the place the brand holds:

choices.f: Always relative to competitors.
Shelf position is distribution, not positioning.
It only matters where customers hold it.

variants.text: Three segments are attractive. Which one do you target first?

choices.t: The one you can win and serve profitably
choices.f: Attractiveness plus your ability to win.
Big but unwinnable wastes money.
Splitting budget weakens every message.

variants.text: Two segments respond the same way to price, packs and ads. Which test fails?

choices.f: If they respond alike, they are one segment.
They can be measured; they just do not differ.
Size is not the issue.
